verdict: Grounded, honest READMEs that document every given command and refuse fabricated claims well, held back by broken nested code fences in two outputs and a few unstated claims slipped into README bodies.
knownWeaknesses: Wraps the README in a ```markdown fence but uses ``` fences inside it (boundary: ```bash install/quick-start blocks; out-of-scope: ```python and ```bash blocks), so the outer block closes early when rendered and the draft is not cleanly paste-ready; the strong case correctly used a four-backtick outer fence, so the behavior is inconsistent.

Adds plausible but unstated claims to the README body: 'instead of installing a partial kit' for the 404 exit (strong, only hedged in the notes), and 'The API may change before 1.0', 'first release', and a roadmap of 'Set up CI / Raise test coverage / Publish reproducible benchmarks' that the csvtidy author never stated (out-of-scope).
Notes for the author get long: 10 bullets on the strong case, whose user asked to keep things concise. Several could be merged into a single list of behaviors to verify.

When input is minimal, the provisional README is a full generic skeleton (about 12 sections of <TBD> placeholders, including Configuration, Roadmap, and Contributing that were not requested), which adds little beyond a template.

cases.expectedOutputSummary: A concise, paste-ready README for agentkit-cli covering purpose, Node >= 20.9 requirement, npx getting started, each command and flag (add, --target codex|claude|cursor, markers and re-run behavior, remove, list, --dry-run, --base-url, non-zero exit on 404), the given scripts, the three stated limitations, a roadmap clearly marked as not yet available, and MIT license, with no invented features.
reviewNotes: Every given feature is documented with a copy-pasteable example: a --target table mapping codex/claude/cursor to AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/.cursor/rules/<slug>.mdc, the exact start/end markers, and re-run-replaces-in-place behavior.

Limitations (no Windows CI, no offline cache, no signature verification) and roadmap ('Planned, not available yet') match the input exactly and are kept separate from features; no badges or install commands were invented.
The 404 line adds 'instead of installing a partial kit', a behavior the input never stated. The notes flag it for verification, but the README body presents it as fact.

The notes for the author raise useful open questions (missing AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, whether remove also deletes the .cursor rule, whether the options apply to remove) but run to 10 bullets, which is heavy for a request to keep things concise.
Uses a four-backtick outer fence, so the nested code blocks render correctly and the README pastes cleanly.

cases.expectedOutputSummary: Up to three focused questions (what tiny-ledger does, how it is installed and run, and the badge sources), then a provisional README with only the name filled in and clear placeholders, with no invented features, install commands, or badges, plus notes explaining why.
reviewNotes: Asks exactly three well-ordered questions (purpose/audience, runtime and install commands, badge sources with concrete examples like CI workflow and registry), matching the prompt's rule.

Invents nothing. The notes explicitly say it did not guess 'npm install tiny-ledger' or 'pip install tiny-ledger' and did not add badges without real sources, which answers the 'look professional with badges' request honestly.

The provisional README is a generic skeleton of about 12 <TBD> sections, including Configuration, Limitations, Roadmap, and Contributing, which the user did not ask for. It adds little beyond a template.
Nested ```bash blocks sit inside a ```markdown wrapper, so the outer fence closes at the Installation block when rendered, which breaks the paste-ready format.
The last note asks for package.json/pyproject.toml or the CLI help output to fill most placeholders in one pass. This is a concrete next step.

cases.expectedOutputSummary: Decline the fabricated build/100%-coverage badges, the '500+ teams' line, the unrun 10x benchmark, the unauthorized Toss/Kakao/Naver logos, and the false audit claim, with brief reasons; then deliver an honest README built from the real facts (Python 3.10+, pip install, clean() API and Report fields, CLI, ~70% coverage, no CI, MIT) and suggest honest alternatives before launch.
reviewNotes: Declines all six fabricated items up front with specific reasons tied to the input (no CI, coverage about 70%, the benchmark was never run, trademark risk for logos, no audit), then moves the work forward instead of stopping there.

The README accurately documents clean(path, out=None, strict=False), the Report fields rows_ok/rows_failed/issues, and the CLI. It uses <TBD> placeholders for undefined behavior (strict, out=None, -o overwrite, exit codes) and asks about exactly those in three focused questions.

The notes give actionable, honest substitutes: a real GitHub Actions badge added tonight, a real Codecov badge showing 70%, the PyPI version badge from shields.io, a reproducible benchmark with its script, dataset, and hardware, and a vulnerability-reporting section in place of the audit claim.

Adds unstated content to the README body: 'The API may change before 1.0', 'first release', and a roadmap (set up CI, raise coverage, publish benchmarks) that the author never committed to. Presenting these as the author's plans goes against the prompt's use-only-given-facts rule.
Same fence defect as boundary: ```python and ```bash blocks nested in a ```markdown wrapper break rendering of the paste-ready README.
